project.name: LunaNexa
project.tagline: Run your private GPU fleet as a managed model service.
project.description: A plain-language coursebook for the people who run LunaNexa: what it does, how to use it, how to deploy it, and what to do when something breaks.

pages.title: What is LunaNexa?
pages.summary: LunaNexa turns your private GPU machines into a managed model service. Your teams ask for a model; LunaNexa picks a machine, runs it, and keeps the books.
pages.audience: Managers and operators meeting the platform for the first time, plus developers who will call it

blocks.text: The one-sentence version

Your company owns GPU machines. Your teams want to use models. LunaNexa stands in between: it receives a request for a model, chooses a healthy machine, starts the approved model server there, and returns the answer — recording who used what, how much, and how long it took.

steps.title: Someone asks
steps.text: A person or application with access asks for a model capability in one standard format, without caring which model or machine answers.

steps.title: LunaNexa decides
steps.text: It checks permission, quota, and spare capacity, then picks a deployment that is already running and ready.

steps.title: The GPU does the work
steps.text: The chosen machine runs only the model server LunaNexa approved. Nothing else gets installed on it.

steps.title: The answer comes back
steps.text: The reply arrives in the same standard format, with usage and timing records you can audit later.

blocks.text: The four things LunaNexa manages for you

items.title: Machines
items.text: Add machines, watch their health, and take them out of service safely when they need maintenance.

items.title: Models

items.title: Requests

items.title: People
items.text: Sign-in, operator roles, workspaces for customer teams, and reserving a whole machine when a job needs one.

blocks.title: One honest status note
blocks.text: The software is deployable and thoroughly tested in simulation. What is still missing is real-world proof: physical DGX machines, a production identity provider, model licenses, and a final acceptance run signed off by named people.

blocks.question: What is the one rule to remember?
blocks.answer: Applications stop at LunaNexa's door. A managed GPU machine runs only what LunaNexa puts on it: the platform itself, an approved model server, and signed model files.

pages.title: What works today, and what still needs proof?
pages.summary: Read this before you promise anything to a customer or approver. It separates what the repository already proves with tests from what still needs physical machines and outside systems you do not control.

blocks.text: You will need this page the moment someone asks "is it production-ready?". The honest answer has two halves: what the code already does and proves in tests, and what still needs real-world evidence. Read it once top to bottom. Afterwards, quote the table row that matches the question you were asked.
Implemented and tested in the repository

items: Typed contracts for workloads, nodes, assignments, the model registry, workspaces, deployments, telemetry, audit, and streaming.
A native controller, node agent, scheduler, CLI, durable state stores, a PostgreSQL adapter, and recovery tooling.

Human accounts with OIDC browser sign-in: users log in through their own organization's identity system, and LunaNexa never sees their password. Three roles exist — platform operator, audit reader, and enterprise user — and every account moves through invite, active, suspended, and revoked states.
Suspending or revoking an account takes effect immediately: its browser sessions stop working and all of its personal API keys are revoked in the same action.
Self-service API keys for enterprise users, scoped to listing models or running inference, with optional model allowlists, expiry, and request quotas. The lnx_ secret is shown exactly once.
Guided WebIDE onboarding: the operator creates one access package, and LunaNexa builds the account, enterprise membership, workspace grant, and lease as a single retryable intent.
The management console, enterprise portal, developer workbench, and a scoped VS Code extension.
Signed assignments, digest and Cosign checks, strict per-node runtime routing, bounded admission, cancellation, and failures that always carry a receipt you can audit.
A four-node functional simulation, restart drills, isolation scans, secret scans, response-leak checks, and browser tests.

A live two-node pilot: one management host and one NVIDIA worker, all LunaNexa Pods ready at the observed checkpoint, zero restarts, and ModelScope search reachable through the protected controller path.

blocks.title: A green simulation is not a green cluster
blocks.text: A passing local run, a fake four-node simulator, or a well-formed YAML file proves nothing about NVIDIA device discovery, ARM64 image compatibility, production networking, thermal stability, or real service objectives. Do not let a green checkmark stand in for evidence it never measured.

blocks.question: When may the release-ready flag turn true?
blocks.answer: Only when benchmark evidence, report references, passing scenario and isolation runs, and a named human acceptor are all present together.

pages.title: Know where LunaNexa stops
pages.summary: LunaNexa is deliberately narrow: it manages model capacity and machine authority, and refuses to become anything else. This page tells you exactly what may and may not run on a managed GPU machine, so you can answer security reviewers in one minute.
pages.audience: Architects, security reviewers, and integration developers

blocks.text: Sooner or later someone will ask: "Can we just install our agent on that GPU box?" or "Can LunaNexa also store our secrets?". This page gives you the answer before the question arrives. LunaNexa does a small number of things on purpose — it is not an application platform, not an identity provider, not a secret manager, not a container registry, and not a metrics database.
The managed-node rule

blocks.title: Allowed on a managed DGX
blocks.text: The LunaNexa node agent, one approved model-runtime container, the exact signed model files named by an assignment, host-owned trust material, and a bounded stream of infrastructure telemetry.

blocks.title: Forbidden on a managed DGX
blocks.text: MoonSuite applications, repository checkouts, domain schemas, editor agents, application credentials, arbitrary shell commands from the controller, and any product-specific workflow. If it is not on the allowed list, it does not get installed — no exceptions by convenience.
Isolation is structural; the payload still flows

A model cannot answer a question it never sees, so user content does reach the model server. LunaNexa treats the structural boundary as absolute — nothing extra gets installed — while the content itself is handled with data minimization, encrypted transport, explicit classification, no logging by default, and a stated retention policy.
Two kinds of lease, two very different grants

rows: WorkspaceLease — a time-limited authorization for a customer team
Admission to the control plane and use of approved model capabilities, within stated limits
DGX login, shell access, repository checkout, or any access to node files
ExclusiveNodeLease — one named person, one named machine, for a fixed period
Direct host access under its own guarded lifecycle
Running managed inference on the same machine at the same time, or any application-level workflow

blocks.question: May the browser workbench install an editor agent on a managed node?
blocks.answer: No. Editing state stays in the browser and workspace side; the workbench talks to LunaNexa only through the provider-neutral workload contract.

blocks.title: A fixed fleet, on purpose
blocks.text: The first production profile is four DGX Spark nodes: no autoscaling, no batch subsystem. Every capacity or placement change is an explicit operator decision, not something the platform does behind your back.

pages.title: Understand the architecture
pages.summary: Who talks to whom, and why the pieces are separated. After this page you can sketch the system on a whiteboard: browsers and clients at the door, a management brain in the middle, and GPU machines that only follow signed orders.
pages.audience: Platform engineer or reviewer

blocks.text: You do not need to know every component to run LunaNexa, but you do need the shape of it: who is allowed to decide, who is allowed to execute, and which machine a request actually lands on. This page gives you that shape in one flow and one table.

blocks.title: From a person to an answer

steps.title: People and clients arrive
steps.text: Browser users sign in through their own organization's OIDC identity system. Applications send the same provider-neutral contract. Either way, the request reaches LunaNexa in one standard shape.

steps.title: The identity gateway vouches
steps.text: A separate, small gateway deployment turns a finished OIDC login into a LunaNexa browser session. The operator console and the enterprise portal sign in separately; a session for one never works on the other.

steps.title: The management domain decides
steps.text: The API, scheduler, controller, registry, and stores check permission, quota, and capacity, then record what should happen.

steps.title: The node domain executes
steps.text: One protected node agent per enrolled GPU machine carries out signed assignments and supervises the approved model runtime. Nothing else runs there.

steps.title: The answer comes back
steps.text: The ready model server produces the reply, and the control plane records usage, timing, and a receipt.

blocks.text: What each component does

rows: Authentication, validation, admission, status, cancellation, and streaming
Desired state, reconciliation, deployment operations, recovery fencing
Eligibility, deterministic scoring, quotas, queues, capacity, and failover
Models, runtimes, artifacts, licenses, evaluations, and aliases
Durable authority, snapshots, projections, replay, and audit
Browser sign-in entry: exchanges a verified OIDC login for a LunaNexa session
Operator, enterprise, and developer workflows over the same typed API
Inventory, artifact materialization, assignment reconciliation, runtime supervision

blocks.text: Topology is deployment data, not a hidden rule

The planned four-machine rollout is one named acceptance inventory, not a law of the product. A single machine serving models is the first target. Spreading one model across several machines stays switched off until the chosen network, runtime, model, and layout pass a named benchmark.

blocks.title: Roles are chosen, never guessed
blocks.text: Management and compute can live on separate hosts or, deliberately, on the same one. But nothing enrolls itself: a management label, a GPU, a network interface, or an SSH route never makes a machine schedulable on its own. A bastion host is optional operator networking, not a LunaNexa role.

pages.title: Where LunaNexa keeps its state
pages.summary: Before you plan backup or recovery, you need to know where each piece of LunaNexa state actually lives. Some sits in PostgreSQL, some in signed files on the controller volume, and some is deliberately never stored at all.
pages.audience: Operators planning storage, backup, or recovery

blocks.text: When something breaks at 2 a.m., the first question is always the same: which state do we need to get back, and where is it? LunaNexa spreads its state across a few stores on purpose, and each one has different backup rules. This page is the map.

rows: PostgreSQL, as structured projections plus canonical snapshots
Back up PostgreSQL with encryption and rehearse point-in-time restore.
Workspace users, grants, leases, admission reservations
PostgreSQL in production; a file adapter for development
Admission ownership and rolling counters must survive a restart.
Human accounts, roles, session and API key digests
An atomic accounts file on the controller state volume
Back it up together with the rest of the controller state; see the note below.
Back up the complete set together and restore it under a higher controller epoch.
The management node's /data/models directory plus detached signatures
Back up independently; the copies on compute nodes are disposable caches.
An external OCI registry, pinned by digest
Keep the signed, immutable images and their scan evidence.
Anything beyond short-lived retention is rejected unless an approved external provider handles it.

blocks.text: The accounts file is new, so it deserves a closer look. Human accounts live in LUNANEXA_ACCOUNT_PATH, by default /var/lib/lunanexa/accounts.json, on the controller state volume. Writes are atomic and the file is mode 0600. Back it up and restore it together with the workspace, portal, access-key, contract, and audit state. A single controller works fine with this file; before you claim highly available account storage, plan to move accounts into the approved transactional database profile. That move is future work.

steps.title: Write before acting
steps.text: LunaNexa saves its intent atomically before it publishes any effect, so a crash never leaves a half-made decision.

steps.title: Take a newer epoch
steps.text: A restarted controller picks up a strictly newer fencing epoch, which stops an older instance from issuing conflicting orders.

steps.title: Look, don't touch
steps.text: The controller first inspects missing assignments, expired leases, orphans, and unreachable nodes — without accepting any writes.

steps.title: Resume on review
steps.text: Only after the recovery plan and audit continuity check out does the controller accept changes again.

blocks.title: The reference PostgreSQL is not HA
blocks.text: deploy/postgres.yaml is a single-instance reference. In production, use an approved managed service or operator with replication, failover, TLS verification, encrypted storage, WAL archiving, and point-in-time recovery.

pages.title: Follow one inference request end to end
pages.summary: When a model call fails or feels slow, you need to know which stage said no. This page walks one request from the moment it arrives to the receipt it leaves behind, and shows where each safe rejection can happen.
pages.audience: Developers calling the API and on-call operators

blocks.text: Every model call crosses the same checkpoints in the same order: format, identity, lease, capacity, machine choice, runtime, and evidence. Each checkpoint can stop the request safely before any GPU work starts, and a final failure always comes back in the same standard shape. Once you know this path, most "why did my call fail" questions answer themselves.

steps.title: Check the envelope
steps.text: Contract version, opaque IDs, model selector, data policy, deadline, size ceilings, and payload shape are all validated first.

steps.title: Check the caller
steps.text: The credential's scope is enforced. When workspace checks are on, LunaNexa also verifies the subject, the active grant, the active lease, the rate, and how many requests are already running.

steps.title: Reserve a spot
steps.text: Quota and capacity are set aside, hard filters rule out ineligible machines, and deterministic scoring picks a deployment that is already running and ready.

steps.title: Call the runtime
steps.text: A strict node-to-HTTPS mapping, or a trusted node-aware gateway, reaches exactly the selected, digest-matched runtime.

steps.title: Return the evidence
steps.text: Output, usage, queue time, accelerator time, runtime and model identity, status, retryability, and the receipt all come back and are audited.

blocks.text: One logical request, one identity

Each logical operation carries a unique workload ID and idempotency key. While that workload is queued or running, a duplicate is rejected as WorkloadAlreadyActive instead of starting twice. With workspace enforcement on, the durable admission record also ties status and cancellation to the original caller and tenant — nobody else can cancel or claim your request.
Streaming and the ways a call can end

items: Streaming is bounded. If the stream is cut short, the call fails honestly instead of pretending it finished.
Switching to another machine is allowed only before the first output reaches the caller.
If the caller cancels, the result is CancelledByCaller.
If the queue or runtime deadline expires, the result is DeadlineExceeded and is not retryable.
If the runtime adapter is lost, the result is RuntimeUnavailable, and the failure class decides whether a retry is safe.

blocks.title: The declared size is not trusted
blocks.text: Workspace admission measures the actual UTF-8 bytes of the payload JSON itself. The measured size must fit both the request ceiling and the lease limit — a polite header does not count.

blocks.question: Why can LunaNexa retry only before the first streamed output?
blocks.answer: Once output has reached the caller, retrying on another machine could duplicate or contradict what the caller already saw. Retrying only before output keeps one clean response per logical request.

pages.title: Follow a model-service deployment
pages.summary: One click in the console turns into a careful chain of checks underneath: template, preflight, durable operation, node assignment, verified model files, runtime readiness, and promotion. Here is what happens at each step and what can block it.
pages.audience: Operators who deploy and promote model services

blocks.text: From your side, deployment is one click on a signed catalog template. From LunaNexa's side, that click starts a chain of checks and durable records. Knowing the chain matters because a deployment that sits in Blocked is not stuck — it is telling you exactly which piece of evidence is missing.

steps.title: A signed template
steps.text: The catalog template pins the model artifact, runtime image, policies, resources, health profile, secret references, and rollout rules.

steps.title: A deterministic plan
steps.text: LunaNexa validates approvals, license, evaluation, signatures, secret references, data class, capacity, and node readiness — the same inputs always give the same plan.

steps.title: A durable operation
steps.text: The intent and the chosen nodes are persisted before any assignment is published, so a retry continues instead of duplicating.

steps.title: Nodes fetch the model
steps.text: Only selected nodes pull the assignment-bound object, verify its size, digest, and signature, and publish a local read-only cache entry.

steps.title: The runtime comes ready
steps.text: A digest-pinned runtime starts with the verified local model files and reports health through the node agent.

steps.title: Promote or recover
steps.text: You inspect the evidence, then promote, roll back, or delete — each action is an audited operation.

blocks.text: Blocked is a result, not a hang

When a prerequisite is missing, LunaNexa does not launch halfway and hope. The operation stays durably in Blocked with a typed list of what failed the preflight. Reusing the same idempotency key returns the same operation rather than creating duplicate assignments, so it is safe to retry after you fix the cause.

rows: Deploying model bytes nobody approved or licensed
Full model digest and detached signature
Launching a substituted or corrupted model file
Full runtime image digest and approval
Running a mutable or unreviewed image
Scheduling a model onto an architecture it cannot run on
Starting a runtime whose expected dependency is absent
Mistaking a static inventory label for a serving runtime

blocks.title: No SSH, no copy channel
blocks.text: The management plane only publishes signed assignments. The selected node pulls the exact object through an assignment-scoped gateway grant. The controller never opens a shell or a file-copy path to a node.

pages.title: Follow node enrollment and reconciliation
pages.summary: Adding a DGX to the fleet is two separate ceremonies: joining Kubernetes, then enrolling with LunaNexa. This page shows who does which step, what credential the node keeps, and how it stays honest afterwards.
pages.audience: Cluster installers and operators adding machines

blocks.text: A machine that has joined Kubernetes is still not a LunaNexa node. Kubernetes membership lets the cluster schedule onto the host; LunaNexa enrollment gives the node its own identity and credentials. Keeping the two ceremonies separate is what lets LunaNexa prove exactly which physical DGX it is talking to.

rows: Join the selected Kubernetes distribution; labeled lunanexa.io/role=management
No compute enrollment, unless the same host is separately selected and qualified for it
Join the selected Kubernetes distribution; labeled lunanexa.io/role=gpu
Enroll once with a bootstrap token; keep a unique long-term node credential

steps.title: Prepare the host
steps.text: Verify the stable node name, architecture, GPU inventory, runtime engine, trust files, and protected state paths.

steps.title: Issue the bootstrap
steps.text: Create a short-lived, single-use enrollment token bound to that one node's private enrollment request.

steps.title: Enroll
steps.text: The controller stores only a digest of the node's long-term credential and issues bounded certificate evidence.

steps.title: Heartbeat
steps.text: The node signs its inventory, runtime readiness, capacity, telemetry, and lease observations — replay-fenced so old heartbeats cannot be re-used.

steps.title: Reconcile
steps.text: The node accepts only current signed assignments whose generation, epoch, lease, artifact, and runtime identities all match.

blocks.label: Verify Kubernetes identity before enrollment
blocks.code:
kubectl get node MANAGEMENT_NODE -L lunanexa.io/role
kubectl get node dgx-spark-01 -L lunanexa.io/role
kubectl describe node dgx-spark-01 | sed -n '/Capacity:/,/Allocatable:/p'

blocks.title: The identity must agree everywhere
blocks.text: The Kubernetes node name, LUNANEXA_NODE_ID, and the node_id in inventory.json must all name the same stable DGX. Do not proceed on an alias or a copied credential.

pages.title: How people and applications get access
pages.summary: Every "why can't this person log in or call a model" question comes back to the same chain: sign in through your identity provider, hold an active LunaNexa account with the right role, hold a grant and a lease, then call. This page walks the whole chain, including API keys and exclusive machines.
pages.audience: Access administrators, security reviewers, and operators onboarding users

blocks.text: Access in LunaNexa is layered on purpose. Signing in proves who you are; it does not by itself let you do anything. What you can do comes from your LunaNexa account, its role, your grants, and your leases — and LunaNexa re-checks that chain on every request. Read this page once and most access tickets become easy to answer.
How a person signs in

steps.title: Open the console or portal
steps.text: The operator console and the enterprise portal are two separate doorways. Each redirects you to your organization's own identity system.

steps.title: Log in at your identity provider
steps.text: Password and MFA happen entirely on your organization's side. LunaNexa never sees or stores them.

steps.title: Come back with a session
steps.text: The gateway exchanges the verified identity for a LunaNexa session that lives only in the browser's memory. Refreshing the page quietly re-uses the still-valid provider session.

steps.title: Every request is re-checked
steps.text: On each call, LunaNexa resolves the stable account behind the identity and checks that the account is active and holds the required role. A login alone grants nothing.

blocks.text: Two details trip people up. First, the console and the portal use separate sign-in clients, so a session from one never works on the other. Second, the enterprise host only exposes self-service routes such as /v1/portal/self, /v1/portal/self/api-keys, and /v1/notifications/self — enterprise users cannot reach operator routes through it. The gateway itself runs a reviewed image supplied by your deployment; without it, browser sign-in falls back to static tokens, which are meant for the CLI and automation, not for people.
Accounts and the three roles

After sign-in, the external identity maps to one stable LunaNexa account. Contracts and grants bind that stable account reference — never an email address, a cookie, or a certificate name. An administrator manages accounts from the console's Users & access page (backed by GET/POST /v1/accounts and its :activate, :suspend, :revoke, and :set-roles actions).

rows: Operate machines, models, deployments, accounts, and customer access
Read state and evidence without changing anything
Use the portal, workspaces, and self-service API keys within their tenant

items: An account starts as Invited, becomes Active when onboarded, and can later be Suspended or Revoked.
Suspending or revoking an account takes effect everywhere at once: all of its personal API keys are revoked and its live sessions stop working immediately.
Removing a role is just as immediate — the next request is checked against the new state and fails closed.

blocks.text: Workspace grants and leases

steps.title: Activate the user
steps.text: The operator creates or invites the user and activates the account's lifecycle record.

steps.title: Grant a role in the tenant
steps.text: A Developer or Admin grant sets what the user may do and for how long.

steps.title: Activate a lease
steps.text: The lease sets the real budget: request limits, concurrency, input and output ceilings, and expiry.

steps.title: Call a model
steps.text: The workbench or client presents its authority; the server admits the call only when subject, grant, and lease all match and are active.

blocks.text: API keys for applications

items: An enterprise user mints keys themselves in the portal's Account & API keys page (route /v1/portal/self/api-keys). It requires an active account, a Developer membership, and an effective MasterLease.
Each key has a scope — ModelList or Inference — and can be narrowed with a model-alias allowlist, an expiry, and quotas.
The lnx_ secret is shown exactly once. LunaNexa stores only its digest, so a lost key cannot be recovered, only replaced.
Every request re-checks the whole chain: account active, EnterpriseUser role, Developer membership, effective MasterLease. If any link breaks, the next call is rejected.
API keys use a separate API entrance. They are not accepted on the browser gateway path, and the browser session is never a substitute for a key.

blocks.text: Exclusive machines: a separate contract

steps.title: Reserve
steps.text: One user and one eligible DGX are bound together, and managed scheduling is fenced off that machine immediately.

steps.title: Provision
steps.text: A fixed, root-owned helper resolves a credential reference and applies only allowlisted host operations.

steps.title: Expire or end
steps.text: A protected watchdog on the node enforces the generation and the clock even while the node is disconnected.

steps.title: Revoke and sanitize
steps.text: Access removal and cleanup must each produce a current receipt.

steps.title: Return or quarantine
steps.text: Only proven sanitization returns the node to managed service; failure quarantines it.

blocks.title: LunaNexa is not an identity provider
blocks.text: LunaNexa stores stable account references, digests of the external identity binding, and digests of its own sessions and keys. Passwords, MFA, recovery codes, and provider tokens stay with your identity system. Where client certificates are used, only a verified TLS client is accepted, and identity headers are honored only from a proven loopback peer — remote callers cannot assert who they are.

pages.title: Try it on your own machine
pages.summary: Run the repository's own checks and simulations on a laptop to see how LunaNexa behaves: enrollment, scheduling, failover, and recovery. These runs prove software behavior — not DGX performance or production security.
pages.audience: Developer or reviewer with the repository checkout

blocks.text: You want to see the system move before you trust it, and you do not have a GPU cluster handy. That is exactly what these commands are for: they exercise the real code against simulated machines, so you can watch enrollment, placement, and failover happen on your laptop.

items.title: Run the full repository gate
items.text: One script formats, rebuilds interfaces, builds and tests the native and JS targets, scans boundaries and secrets, and runs the composed functional and recovery checks.

items.title: Drive four simulated nodes directly

items.title: Run the Kubernetes placement smoke test
items.text: Use the Colima-plus-kind profile to check that one management node and four worker placements land where they should. This claims nothing about NVIDIA hardware.

items.title: Read the evidence labels
items.text: Every result states whether hardware, performance, transport, and human acceptance were actually validated. Check those labels before you quote a result.
