blocks.text: The last command shows exactly one Ready management node and four Ready workers labeled gpu. This was exercised on an Apple-silicon Mac with Colima. It is a placement simulation: no NVIDIA device and no production identity was involved.

blocks.title: Read the evidence, not just the exit code
blocks.text: The simulator deliberately records hardware_performance_validated: false in its output. That line is the honest part — do not remove it, and do not talk yourself into reading it as anything else.

pages.title: Use the management console
pages.summary: The console is where you run the cluster day to day: check posture, manage nodes and models, manage user accounts, and give customers WebIDE access. This page walks you through the screens in the order you will actually use them.
pages.audience: LunaNexa operator

blocks.text: The console is your daily driver. This page teaches the habits that keep you out of trouble — sign in correctly, read before you click, confirm before you commit — and then covers the two jobs people ask about most: managing user accounts, and getting a customer developer into their desktop IDE.

items.title: Sign in the right way
items.text: With OIDC enabled, the console sends you to your organization's identity system and brings you back with a LunaNexa session. Without OIDC, use the static operator token through trusted ingress. Never expose the controller's HTTP listener directly.

items.title: Read the Overview first
items.text: Before changing anything, confirm cluster posture, capacity, queues, alerts, and recent changes. Thirty seconds here prevents most mistakes.

items.title: Open the evidence behind a state
items.text: A green label is a summary, not proof. Open the assignment, model, deployment, request, or audit detail and look at the current receipt and source state.

items.title: Respect the confirmation prompts
items.text: Cordon, drain, rollback, revoke, suspend, and early lease termination show you the blast radius and ask for an explicit confirmation. Read the scope before you type it.

items.title: Watch the change land
items.text: After any action, follow it through operation, assignment, node heartbeat, runtime readiness, and the audit receipt, until desired and actual state agree.

blocks.alt: The live LunaNexa management console in Simplified Chinese, showing the overview dashboard before a controller is connected.
blocks.caption: Real browser capture of the management console. The disconnected state is intentional: the UI does not invent node or model health before it receives controller data.

items.title: Nodes
items.text: Health, inventory, labels, workloads, cordon, drain, and lease mode.

items.title: Models
items.text: Artifact, license, evaluation, compatibility, aliases, and approval.

items.title: Catalog & deployments
items.text: Templates, preflight, durable service operations, promotion, rollback, and delete.

items.title: Users & access
items.text: Create human accounts, assign one of the three roles, and activate, suspend, or revoke. Suspending or revoking also ends the person's sessions and personal API keys on the spot. Workspace leases and grants live here too.

items.title: Requests
items.text: Aggregate latency, throughput, errors, queueing, and bounded request detail.

items.title: Audit & evidence
items.text: Actor, policy, target, prior/next state, result, correlation, benchmarks, and export.

blocks.text: Give a customer developer WebIDE access

items: Open Users & access and choose Create WebIDE access.

Enter the identity-provider subject you have verified with the customer by hand, plus the person's name, organization, and tenant. Pick the reviewed developer template and an access period of at most 365 days.

Review the derived scope and confirm. LunaNexa creates the account, enterprise membership, workspace grant, and requested lease as one intent — if something interrupts it, the same action safely resumes.
When the customer's master agreement takes effect, choose Enable WebIDE on the same page. LunaNexa refuses to switch it on while any prerequisite is missing.

blocks.title: The five milestones both of you can see

steps.title: Identity
steps.text: The person's sign-in is linked to a stable LunaNexa account.

steps.title: Organization access
steps.text: Enterprise membership and the developer role are in place.

steps.title: Contract
steps.text: The customer's master agreement is signed and effective.

steps.title: Workspace and models
steps.text: The lease and the approved model aliases are granted.

steps.title: Desktop connection
steps.text: The user opens the Desktop IDE page and starts their local IDE with a one-time, roughly two-minute handoff.

blocks.title: Language support
blocks.text: The console and workbench support English and Simplified Chinese through one shared browser locale preference, while protocol IDs and operator-entered technical values stay untouched.

pages.title: Use the developer workbench and editor clients
pages.summary: The workbench is where developers edit and call models from the browser. This page covers how a user gets WebIDE access in the first place, what the workbench shows, and how external editors connect — with credentials that never leak into the wrong hands.
pages.audience: Developers with a workspace lease, and the operators who onboard them

blocks.text: Before anyone can use the workbench, an operator has to open the door and the user has to walk through it. The good news: the operator side is one form and one later click, and the user side shows a single to-do at a time. Here is the whole journey, then how the workbench itself behaves.
Opening the door: the operator side

items: Open Users & access in the console and choose Create WebIDE access.
Enter the identity-provider subject you have verified with the person, plus their name, organization, and tenant. Pick the reviewed WebIDE developer template and an access period of at most 365 days.

Review the derived scope and create the package. LunaNexa builds the account, enterprise membership, workspace user, Developer grant, and requested lease as one retryable whole — a safe retry continues instead of duplicating.

When the customer's MasterLease is effective, choose Enable WebIDE. The overview shows five milestones — identity, organization access, contract, workspace and models, desktop connection — so you can see exactly what is still missing.

blocks.text: Walking through: the enterprise user side

items: Sign in to the portal with your organization's identity provider.
Follow the readiness page. It shows one blocking to-do at a time — for example completing the MasterLease — instead of a wall of status.
Open Desktop IDE, review the granted tenant, models, and expiry, then choose Open desktop WebIDE.

Wait for the one-time handoff, roughly 120 seconds. It launches your local MoonCode through MoonGate and installs a lease-scoped lunanexa-lease provider. The reusable secret is never exposed to the browser.

blocks.text: Using the workbench day to day

items.title: Connect identity
items.text: The browser reads /v1/workspace/self through trusted ingress and displays the mapped subject's current authorization.

items.title: Confirm active capability
items.text: A valid user, tenant grant, active time window, and TextGenerate lease must agree before Send is enabled.

items.title: Edit locally
items.text: Project drafts stay in the browser. The workbench is not a remote DGX filesystem or a shell.

items.title: Invoke explicitly
items.text: Each call is a standard short-lived request with bounded input and output and a unique workload and idempotency identity.

items.title: Inspect the evidence
items.text: Read the output, status, usage, timing, and receipt. If a lease expires mid-session, the server's rejection is the final word.

blocks.alt: The live LunaNexa developer workbench in Simplified Chinese, showing its access gate and browser-local workspace shell.
blocks.caption: Real browser capture of the developer workbench before a workspace token is provided. The access gate remains separate from the model editor.

blocks.text: External editors

rows: Working scoped client over explicitly selected text
Token in SecretStorage, bound to the approved origin and machine-scoped settings
Vendor credentials and the agent runtime stay with the external client
Bearer credential stays in browser memory for the active session

blocks.title: Session fields are not inference enforcement yet
blocks.text: max_active_sessions and max_session_duration_ms are validated policy for a future server-side WorkspaceSession service. Today's inference enforcement uses per-capability request concurrency and rate limits.

pages.title: Integrate a provider-neutral client
pages.summary: Your application talks to LunaNexa through one stable request contract, with an API key you can trace back to a person and a lease. This page shows how to get that key, what the contract asks of your client, and what must never go into a request.
pages.audience: Developers integrating an application or provider router with LunaNexa

blocks.text: LunaNexa deliberately speaks one request language. Your application never sends product-specific assumptions or its own identity system to the cluster — it sends one standard envelope, and LunaNexa decides the rest. Compatibility APIs that mimic other providers exist, but they are adapters on top of this contract, not the source of truth.
Get a credential first

rows: A person using the console or portal
Sign in through your organization's identity provider; the session lives only in browser memory
Self-service in the portal's Account & API keys page, if your account is active, holds a Developer membership, and your organization has an effective MasterLease

items: A key has a scope — ModelList or Inference — and can be narrowed with a model-alias allowlist, an expiry, and quotas.
The secret is shown exactly once at creation. LunaNexa stores only its digest, so save it somewhere safe; a lost key is replaced, not recovered.
Every request re-checks the full chain behind the key: account active, EnterpriseUser role, Developer membership, effective MasterLease. If any link breaks, calls fail immediately.
API keys use a separate API entrance, not the browser gateway path. Keep the key in your secret store and never commit it.

blocks.text: What your client must do

items: Translate your application's authority and data policy into the generic WorkloadEnvelope on your side, before the request reaches LunaNexa.
Use opaque tenant, workload, correlation, and idempotency values that reveal nothing about your product.
Select a published model alias or capability — never a repository path or an internal node address.
Respect the typed answers: whether a failure is retryable, the deadlines, cancellation, and the receipt that comes with every final result.
Keep provider fallback and application policy in your own repository.

blocks.title: Never put these in the workload
blocks.text: Application credentials, repository paths, product names, editor state, internal runtime URLs, node credentials, or secret-provider values.

pages.title: Deploy management first, then explicitly selected compute
pages.summary: The installation order that keeps you safe: stand up and verify the management foundation through the guarded UI, optionally add browser sign-in, then qualify and enroll only the compute machines you deliberately choose.
pages.audience: Named deployment operator

blocks.text: You are about to install the real thing, so order matters. Management, storage, and compute are separate roles, and you bring them up in that order: the management foundation first and verified, browser sign-in when you are ready for human users, and compute machines only after each one earns its place. A lab host may carry temporary compute; a bastion is just your own networking, not a LunaNexa role.

steps.title: Prepare the chosen host
steps.text: Join it to your Kubernetes distribution, find its real node name, prepare /data/models, pin the SSH host identity, and note whether storage is dedicated or temporary.

steps.title: Render the management manifests
steps.text: Build immutable images, render management.yaml, and generate a separate mode-0600 secret manifest. Secret values never touch the browser.

steps.title: Preview in the UI
steps.text: Choose Management foundation, enter host and file references only, and run Preview. It proves SSH, storage, Kubernetes, CoreDNS, and metrics access without changing anything, then lists which non-secret resources would differ. The protected Secret manifest is never diffed.

steps.title: Confirm and apply
steps.text: After reviewing the Preview, type the exact confirmation phrase. Apply labels only the selected management node and reconciles the manifests you reviewed.

steps.title: Verify every service
steps.text: Require PostgreSQL, controller, console, enterprise, and workbench rollouts, each with ready endpoints. Use protected port-forwarding until the TLS edge is reviewed.

steps.title: Qualify compute separately
steps.text: An Ascend host may enter an explicit temporary-compute qualification profile. Future DGX Spark hosts are enrolled only after their own accelerator, runtime, trust, and heartbeat evidence passes.

blocks.label: Render the non-secret management manifest
blocks.code:
scripts/deploy/render-management-foundation.sh \
  --output /ABSOLUTE/RENDERED_DIRECTORY \
  --management-node KUBERNETES_NODE_NAME \
  --control-image IMMUTABLE_CONTROL_IMAGE \
  --web-image IMMUTABLE_WEB_IMAGE \
  --postgres-image IMMUTABLE_POSTGRES_IMAGE \
  --model-store-root /data/models \
  --control-uid MODEL_STORE_UID --control-gid MODEL_STORE_GID \
  --runtime-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:19090/v1/responses \
  --controller-epoch 1

blocks.label: Generate the protected management secret manifest
blocks.code:
scripts/deploy/generate-management-secrets.sh \
  /ABSOLUTE/PROTECTED/management-secrets.yaml
# The generator creates mode 0600 and refuses overwrite.

blocks.text: Run the guarded UI workflow

blocks.label: Open the installer without printing its bearer
blocks.code:
# Terminal 1
sh scripts/build-browser-bundles.sh
python3 -m http.server 4173 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory _build/browser-dist

# Terminal 2: choose a new protected path
LUNANEXA_INSTALLER_TOKEN_FILE=/ABSOLUTE/PROTECTED/session-token \
  sh scripts/start-deployment-ui.sh
# Open http://127.0.0.1:4173/installer/

blocks.label: Management UI fields (references only)
blocks.code:
Deployment target: Management foundation
SSH user and port: selected host login
Private key / known_hosts: absolute operator-machine paths
Management Kubernetes node: exact kubectl node name
Management SSH host: direct host or operator-owned OpenSSH alias
Kubeconfig / rendered directory: absolute operator-machine paths
Protected management secret manifest: absolute mode-0600 file path
Confirmation: leave empty until Preview succeeds

blocks.title: No access-node assumption
blocks.text: Connect directly or use your own VPN or SSH jump host. A bastion is never registered as management or compute, and daily browser, API, and node-agent traffic does not need one.

blocks.title: Roles are explicit, never inferred
blocks.text: Having a GPU does not silently make a management host schedulable. Co-located temporary compute needs its own qualification and enrollment decision. The planned four-DGX rollout is a named acceptance inventory, not a fixed node-count rule of the platform.

blocks.title: The current Ascend 310P3 host is not compute-ready
blocks.text: The device itself is healthy, but Kubernetes exposes no Ascend resource and LunaNexa's telemetry and runtime supervision are still NVIDIA-specific, so compute Preview fails closed. Do not upgrade CANN or enroll the host until the reviewed runtime, device plugin, LunaNexa adapters, reboot recovery, and model evidence all pass.

blocks.title: Stay inside the installer's boundary
blocks.text: The UI starts only after hosts have joined Kubernetes. Preview is read-only and shows a bounded, non-secret change plan; a diff it cannot summarize blocks Apply. Apply needs the scope-specific phrase. The companion accepts no arbitrary shell, no browser-pasted private key, no join token, and no secret value.
Add browser sign-in (OIDC) when humans come aboard

items: Register two OIDC clients with your organization's identity provider: one for the operator console host, one for the enterprise portal host. Sessions never cross between them.
Provision the secret lunanexa-identity-ingress-credentials through your secret manager. It holds the two client credentials, the cookie secrets, and the identity-assertion secret.

Render the overlay: scripts/deploy/render-oidc-browser-ingress.sh combines deploy/oidc-browser-ingress.yaml and deploy/oidc-browser-ingress-controller-patch.yaml with your already-rendered management manifest into one reviewed file. Apply the combined file, never the raw patch.
Pin the identity gateway image by digest. That image is supplied by your deployment — it is reviewed separately and is not built from this repository.
Let the standard secrets generator add account-session-issuer-secret to the controller credentials; it is required for browser sessions and stays out of the gateway.
Include the account store in your backups: it lives at LUNANEXA_ACCOUNT_PATH=/var/lib/lunanexa/accounts.json on the controller state volume.
Without this overlay, only static tokens remain, for the CLI and automation. The static-token browser path is for local acceptance only — never for a public deployment.

blocks.text: Onboard ModelScope models from the protected console

items: Open the deployed console through localhost port-forwarding or reviewed HTTPS. Public plaintext HTTP deliberately disables credential entry.
Sign in with separate operator and audit authorities. Search the ModelScope catalog by model name; do not paste registry JSON.
Open the exact owner/repository row and inspect revision, license, task, and declared size before selecting Download.
Watch the automatically refreshed durable import. A retry resumes verified files or the remaining byte range and never publishes partial bytes.
After source checksums pass, inspect the license, signature, evaluation, and runtime-template gates separately. Approve for users stays disabled until all four are backed by real evidence.

blocks.title: Current MiniCPM pilot state
blocks.text: OpenBMB/MiniCPM5-1B is a public, Apache-2.0 candidate of roughly 2.17 GB. A manual staging directory is not a catalog approval. The first protected UI import must retain the observed revision and per-file hashes, then remain invisible to users until artifact packaging, signature, evaluation, and a qualified serving template exist.

pages.title: Qualify vLLM or SGLang on DGX Spark
pages.summary: Before LunaNexa trusts a model runtime, prove it on real hardware. These single-node templates run vLLM or SGLang on a real ARM64 DGX Spark with a verified local model directory — a proving ground, not a second production deployment path.
pages.audience: Runtime qualification owner

blocks.text: Use this page when you want hard evidence that vLLM or SGLang actually works on your DGX Spark before LunaNexa trusts it. The repository ships single-node templates that need no secrets and exercise a real ARM64 machine with a verified local model directory. Treat them as a proving ground — they are not a second way to deploy to production.
Before you start

items: Record the DGX OS, kernel, ARM64 architecture, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, and container runtime versions.
The NVIDIA device plugin exposes nvidia.com/gpu, and a nvidia RuntimeClass exists — or the reviewed overlay uses the cluster default.
The node is labelled lunanexa.io/role=gpu and pinned by its exact kubernetes.io/hostname.
A verified Hugging Face-format model directory lives only on that DGX, under /var/lib/lunanexa/qualification-models/sha256/<digest>/model.
The runtime image is built for ARM64, signed, scanned, and pinned by its full SHA-256 digest.

rows: 1 GPU, TP=1, bfloat16, 80% of GPU memory, 8192 context
OpenAI-compatible chat; Responses compatibility must be proven or adapted
1 GPU, TP=1, bfloat16, 80% static memory, 8192 context

blocks.label: The qualification sequence
blocks.code:
kubectl apply -f deploy/dgx-spark/runtime-qualification-prerequisites.yaml
kubectl apply -f RENDERED_VLLM.yaml
kubectl -n lunanexa-runtime-qualification rollout status deployment/vllm-dgx-spark --timeout=30m
kubectl -n lunanexa-runtime-qualification logs deployment/vllm-dgx-spark --tail=200

blocks.title: One gap to close before production
blocks.text: Today LunaNexa's materializer publishes a single verified artifact file, but vLLM and SGLang expect a whole Hugging Face directory. Before this can go to production, someone must build and review an adapter that unpacks the directory per assignment and re-verifies the result before mounting it.

blocks.title: LunaFlux is a candidate, not a runtime yet
blocks.text: LunaFlux passed the physical CUDA inventory and some isolated kernel fixtures on the temporary RTX 5060 Ti, but there is no promoted Linux/CUDA image digest and no complete model rollout unit. Matching a schema and passing individual kernels is not end-to-end inference. Add a LunaNexa template only when the exact image, launch and model configuration, listener, live readiness, and correctness and soak evidence are all on file.
Evidence to keep

items: Exact digests for the runtime image, the model tree or archive, and the detached signatures.
Cold and warm start times, time to first token, p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens per second, and memory pressure.
Bad-behavior tests: malformed input, invalid model, cancellation, concurrency saturation, OOM rejection, process restart, and node drain.
One successful LunaNexa request routed through the approved HTTPS boundary, with its streaming receipt.

pages.title: Daily operations: the five jobs you will actually do
pages.summary: A hands-on runbook for the two people who use LunaNexa every day — the operator behind the console and the customer behind the portal. What to do when an alert fires, when an order needs paper, and when a machine lease ends.
pages.audience: On-call operators, customer administrators, finance coordinators, and users of exclusive machines

blocks.text: First, know which screen shows what

rows: The alert center: severity, acknowledge, assign, silence, resolve, plus the source receipt and delivery status
A portal inbox with messages about agreements, payment, documents, leases, access, expiry, and termination, each read or unread
The event stream, metrics, audit receipts, and alert codes
Only the status and reference number for their own request
Quote, approval, document generation, review, correction, and fulfillment controls
Their order timeline, whether the print packet is ready, upload requests, evidence status, and correction requests
Lease state, forced-revocation policy, reachability, wiping, and quarantine
Their machine's display name, username, handoff status, expiry, the end-access action, and wiping status
Signed-in aggregate health, active alert codes, state counts, recovery backlog, and runbook links
The public coursebook and the read-only Ask guide — no live cluster state

blocks.title: One event, two audiences
blocks.text: The same underlying event can show up as an alert for the operator and as a message in the customer's inbox. Reading or dismissing a message never erases the original record, and retrying a failed delivery does not create a second business event.
Job 1: an alert fires — triage it and keep the customer informed

items: Operator: open the alert center and sort Critical and High first. Before changing anything, open the alert and copy its reference number.

Operator: look at the current evidence, then acknowledge the alert so the team knows you own it, and assign it to a specific person. Silence it only when a planned maintenance window explains the signal.
Operator: resolve the alert only after the underlying condition has actually recovered. Resolving closes the alert but keeps its evidence.
Customer: open Notifications in the portal, check that the message concerns your order or lease, follow the suggested action, and mark it read.
If email, SMS, or webhook delivery fails, the in-app record is still the source of truth; the operator investigates the DeliveryDeadLetter alert.

blocks.label: Operator read-only triage (credentials come from the secret provider)
blocks.code:
set -eu
: "${LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT:?set the approved LunaNexa API origin}"
: "${LUNANEXA_OPERATOR_TOKEN:?load operator authority without printing it}"
: "${LUNANEXA_MONITORING_TOKEN:?load monitoring authority without printing it}"

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LUNANEXA_OPERATOR_TOKEN" \
  "$LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT/v1/notifications/operator"

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LUNANEXA_MONITORING_TOKEN" \
  "$LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT/v1/observability/events"

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LUNANEXA_MONITORING_TOKEN" \
  "$LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT/metrics"

blocks.text: Job 2: find out what actually happened

blocks.title: How a signal becomes an alert

steps.title: An event is written
steps.text: A component records what happened as structured data: a stable event code, the outcome, the component, the time, and a reference number.

steps.title: Metrics move
steps.text: Counters and gauges update. They never carry tenant, user, or request identifiers, so they stay small and safe to aggregate.

steps.title: A rule notices
steps.text: A rule based on state or metrics — never on reading log text — decides that this condition matters.

steps.title: An alert opens
steps.text: Repeated signals are folded into one operator record instead of paging you twice for the same problem.

steps.title: Everything is linked
steps.text: For important changes, the audit record shows who acted, what the state was before and after, and the result.

blocks.title: Logs explain; they do not authorize
blocks.text: Use the reference number to connect the alert, the event, and the audit record. Never paste raw logs, tokens, document contents, prompts, model output, SSH material, or callback bodies into a ticket or into the guide.
Job 3: finish an order that needs paper — quote, seal, payment, invoice

blocks.title: From online order to activated service

steps.title: Configure online
steps.text: The customer picks the service, SLA, project, and requested expiry in the portal; the platform fills in who they are.

steps.title: Prepare the paperwork
steps.text: The operator applies the frozen quote and approved policy, gets internal approval, and releases only the verified print files.

steps.title: Sign and pay offline
steps.text: The customer prints the PDF and follows their organization's normal seal, payment, and invoicing process.

steps.title: Upload the proof
steps.text: The customer requests a short-lived upload grant. Object storage and the scanner verify the file's digest and safety; the browser cannot swap in a different file reference.

steps.title: A second person checks
steps.text: A reviewer who did not upload the evidence accepts or rejects the exact file. Rejection keeps the history and asks for a corrected version.

steps.title: Service switches on
steps.text: Only when every required agreement, payment, invoice, identity, and approval item is accepted does the operator activate the entitlement.

blocks.label: Customer and operator read-only order checks
blocks.code:
set -eu
: "${LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT:?set the approved LunaNexa API origin}"
: "${LUNANEXA_INFERENCE_TOKEN:?load customer API authority without printing it}"
: "${LUNANEXA_OPERATOR_TOKEN:?load operator authority without printing it}"
: "${LUNANEXA_CLIENT_CERT_PATH:?set the verified client certificate path}"
: "${LUNANEXA_CLIENT_KEY_PATH:?set the protected client key path}"

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  --cert "$LUNANEXA_CLIENT_CERT_PATH" --key "$LUNANEXA_CLIENT_KEY_PATH" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LUNANEXA_INFERENCE_TOKEN" \
  "$LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT/v1/offline-commerce/self/orders"

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LUNANEXA_OPERATOR_TOKEN" \
  "$LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT/v1/offline-commerce/operator/snapshot"

blocks.title: A generated file is not a legal or financial result
blocks.text: The PDF is a print copy and the DOCX an editable draft. An upload is not an e-signature, a receipt is not money in the bank, and generated metadata is not a tax invoice. Keep the order on hold until your authorized legal and finance reviewers accept the evidence.
Job 4: use an exclusive machine — and hand it back cleanly

items: Customer: before connecting, open Machine access and check the lease state, machine display name, username, reachability, handoff state, start time, and expiry. The portal deliberately never shows the physical node ID or a raw password.

Customer: follow the handoff reference to the approved credential broker or SSH certificate service. That separate, trusted system gives you the host alias, port, certificate, and host-key fingerprint — compare the fingerprint on first login.
Customer: before ending access yourself, save your work and stop your own processes. Check the current lease generation, type the exact confirmation the portal asks for, and submit once.
Operator: watch the machine move through Draining, RevokingAccess, and Sanitizing. Do not put it back into service just because the customer account disappeared.
Operator: return the machine to the pool only after the current wiping receipt checks out. If cleanup fails, quarantine the machine and raise the alert.

blocks.label: Customer read-only access and notification checks
blocks.code:
set -eu
: "${LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT:?set the approved LunaNexa API origin}"
: "${LUNANEXA_INFERENCE_TOKEN:?load customer API authority without printing it}"
: "${LUNANEXA_CLIENT_CERT_PATH:?set the verified client certificate path}"
: "${LUNANEXA_CLIENT_KEY_PATH:?set the protected client key path}"

for path in /v1/machine-access/self /v1/notifications/self; do
  curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
    --cert "$LUNANEXA_CLIENT_CERT_PATH" --key "$LUNANEXA_CLIENT_KEY_PATH" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $LUNANEXA_INFERENCE_TOKEN" \
    "$LUNANEXA_ENDPOINT$path"
done

blocks.title: Exclusive does not mean root
blocks.text: An exclusive lease gives the customer their own non-root account with a documented filesystem boundary and rootless containers. It does not include sudo, access to management machines, LunaNexa's own credentials, other customers' data, or any way to disable the expiry guard on the machine.
Job 5: ask the guide for help — without crossing role lines

rows: Explanations and citations from the published coursebook
Live cluster state, private evidence, raw logs, credentials, or the ability to run operator actions
Aggregate health, active alert codes and counts, node and lease state counts, recovery backlog, knowledge revision, skill names and versions, and runbook links
Node, user, or lease identifiers; alert bodies; prompts; model answers; raw logs; secrets; or any mutation
Skill ID, version, audience, required evidence, allowed tools and data, and the matching runbook page
Tool credentials, unrestricted controller routes, private source paths, or an execution channel

blocks.label: Check coursebook health, then open authenticated admin diagnostics on macOS
blocks.code:
set -eu
: "${LUNANEXA_COURSEBOOK_ORIGIN:?set the approved coursebook origin}"

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  "$LUNANEXA_COURSEBOOK_ORIGIN/health"
open "$LUNANEXA_COURSEBOOK_ORIGIN/admin.html"

blocks.title: Never hand-craft administrator headers
blocks.text: Open administrator diagnostics only through the trusted, signed identity proxy. If that proxy, the internal HTTPS diagnostics gateway, or its secret references are missing, leave admin diagnostics switched off — the public coursebook and the read-only guide still work.
Before go-live: external pieces your deployment must provide

rows: Approved email, SMS, or webhook senders, secret references, a retry policy, and someone who owns dead letters
Rely on the built-in inbox and alert center; do not promise external delivery
A Prometheus-compatible collector, a log collector, protected retention, dashboards, and paging integration
Local metrics, events, audit, and operator alerts still work; long-term history and paging do not
Approved bilingual legal templates, object storage, short-lived upload exchange, a malware scanner, deterministic DOCX/PDF rendering, XLSX checks, callback identity, and legal/finance policy owners
You can demonstrate the workflow only; do not claim settlement, invoicing, or entitlement readiness
A production identity provider, trusted ingress, a credential broker or SSH CA, DNS host aliases, protected provisioning and watchdog, session revocation, and tested wiping and quarantine
Do not offer customer machine login at all
A trusted identity proxy, matching HMAC key, internal HTTPS read-only diagnostics gateway, secret-backed controller authority, network policy, and freshness monitoring
Keep administrator diagnostics off; the public documentation remains available

blocks.question: Before you resolve an alert, what must you check?
blocks.answer: Make sure the underlying condition has really recovered, then use the alert's reference number to connect it with the event, the relevant metric, and the audit record. A customer reading the message, or a delivery succeeding, is not proof of recovery.

pages.title: UI-only end-to-end acceptance SOP
pages.summary: Walk the whole acceptance journey by hand — installer, operator console, enterprise portal, MoonLeaf contract workspace, machine access, workbench, and coursebook — clicking what a real user would click, never substituting API calls for user actions.
pages.audience: Release operator, acceptance tester, customer administrator, and deployment owner

blocks.text: Before you start

blocks.title: Know what this run proves
blocks.text: This SOP proves the browser workflows and a five-node Colima/kind simulation. The demo records you will see never touch a production controller, never issue a real SSH certificate, never execute a legal contract or settle a payment, and say nothing about NVIDIA hardware. Only when identity, secrets, external adapters, PostgreSQL, and physical-node prerequisites are ready do you repeat the same UI sequence against the production origin.

rows: Deployment mode and controller connection form

blocks.text: 1. Create the minimal local cluster from the installer

items: Open the cluster installer and choose Local Colima simulation.
Enter the test-only installer token that the local companion process gives you. Never reuse an operator, inference, monitoring, callback, or production token here.

Click Preview and verify. Confirm the embedded terminal says the dedicated Colima profile is ready — or will start during apply — and that the required tools are installed. The simulator's fixed one-plus-four inventory is a test fixture, not a production topology default.
Enter the exact confirmation RECONCILE SIMULATION.
Click Reconcile simulation. Keep the page open while the embedded terminal streams progress.
For this simulator fixture only, accept when the terminal reports its management and compute placements, all placement probes running, context kind-lunanexa-sim, and command exited successfully.

blocks.title: Recovery behavior worth knowing
blocks.text: The installer starts a stopped dedicated Colima profile during apply, and recreates an unhealthy existing lunanexa-sim topology. Preview stays read-only throughout. If either repair fails, the terminal stays in its failed state and you must not continue.
2. Walk every operator-console page

rows: Cluster running normally; 4/4 machine posture and deployment gate
Acknowledge, assign, silence, resolve, and redrive are consequential controls; use them only on the selected record
Cordon and Drain controls on each node
Model service catalog and service operations
Deploy model service, Promote, Roll back, Delete
End and clean up, End lease, Activate
Digital agreement lifecycle and enterprise requests
Retry reversal, confirm access revoked or still active, request correction, accept exact digest
Contract information, governance, approval queue, form and preview
Choose forms, save data, replace packet
Correlate actor, state transition, result, and receipt

blocks.text: 3. Walk every enterprise-portal page

rows: From agreement signing to an isolated GPU workspace
Request a time-bounded workspace and request history
Redeem SSH access credential; End access early
Refresh, upload evidence, cancel order, download verified file
Contract information and documents with MoonLeaf preview
Disable email, enable email, mark read

blocks.text: 4. Verify the MoonLeaf contract workspace

rows: NVIDIA DGX Spark compute-device remote lease agreement
Equipment damage liability and compensation notice

items: In the operator console, open Contract records. Click each form tab and wait for its MoonLeaf preview; no tab may show MoonLeaf demo preview failed.
Open Early termination application. Enter the operator-owned settlement values: actual rent 1000, paid rent 1200, refund, refund amount 200, and an operator review decision.
Do not enter customer-owned identity, request reason, or signature fields from the operator side. Open the enterprise Contract forms page to complete only the customer-owned fields.
Confirm the preview refreshes on its own without clicking Render current draft, that Chinese characters and spacing look right, and that the new values appear.
Click Save data and confirm the preview and draft values stay stable after the save.

In the operator task inbox, select a tenant, search by packet or order, open a pending approval, and verify the confirmation shows the action, initiator, expected revision, amount, packet-values digest, evidence, and reason before Approve or Reject is enabled.

In the enterprise portal, confirm the same packet shows approval progress, payment and acceptance obligations, readable dates and CNY amounts, and the expiry countdown — with no operator decision button anywhere. Click Send reminder once and confirm the success notice.

Back in the operator console, click Export audit report and inspect the downloaded tenant-scoped JSON: it may contain governance records and value-free lifecycle events, but never tokens, credentials, raw document values, signatures, seals, prompts, or outputs.

blocks.text: 5. End machine access, then inspect the workbench gate

items: In the enterprise portal, click My machines. Confirm the card shows Online, a username, a whole-machine SSH profile, about one day remaining, credential handoff Available, and End access early.
Click End access early, enter the exact displayed phrase TERMINATE exclusive-lease-demo, then click Terminate access.

In demo acceptance, confirm the card changes to Expiring, credential handoff Closed, cleanup Revoking access, and the termination button disappears. In production, keep watching until sanitization evidence closes the lease and the operator returns the node to managed service.

In the demo operator console, open Leases, click End and clean up, review the exact lease, node, user, and generation in the destructive-action dialog, then click Confirm action. Confirm the demo explicitly says it was previewed and no change was persisted.

Open WebIDE. Confirm Connect / refresh is disabled until a scoped inference token is present. Expand Advanced connection settings and verify the controller endpoint and loopback-only opaque subject fields are visible.
Never expect the workbench lease to grant SSH, an arbitrary shell, a repository checkout, or managed-node filesystem access; those remain separate from exclusive-machine access.

blocks.text: 6. Renewal, contract close, and machine reclamation

items: In Contract forms, open Contract packet and select Signed and effective · packet-demo-effective.
Confirm the effective record says read-only and every customer field is disabled; historical contract data must not be edited in place.
Click Request renewal. In the confirmation dialog, review the carry-forward boundary, then click Request renewal once.

Confirm a new Information draft packet is selected, the preceding effective packet remains in the switcher, the customer-owned organization value is carried forward, and the success notice states that demo mode did not contact a controller.

steps.title: Effective contract
steps.text: Both roles complete only their own fields; approvals, exact artifacts, and offline evidence make the contract effective.

steps.title: Renewal or amendment
steps.text: Before expiry, the customer requests renewal or an amendment; the operator reviews the new version, price, term, obligations, and second-person approval when required.

steps.title: Close proposal
steps.text: Expiry, early termination, or a default notice creates a close proposal and a settlement draft from the ledger — access never just silently ends.

steps.title: Revoke and sanitize
steps.text: The controller closes credential handoff, revokes sessions, drains personal processes, sanitizes the host, and quarantines it on any failed evidence.

steps.title: Reclaim
steps.text: Only a verified current-generation sanitization receipt lets the operator return the machine to managed scheduling and close the contract record.

blocks.title: What local UI acceptance cannot prove
blocks.text: The browser demo verifies the renewal, close, and reclamation controls and how states are presented. It cannot manufacture a second human approval, a legal seal, a payment, an external credential issuer, a root-helper receipt, or physical sanitization. Production acceptance must retain those exact external receipts.
Stop conditions and recovery

rows: Start or repair the dedicated profile, then preview again
Use Reconcile simulation; the installer recreates only the dedicated lunanexa-sim cluster
MoonLeaf preview fails, loses Chinese, or shows the wrong form
Do not generate or approve documents
Keep the exact template and values, repair rendering/fonts, switch tabs, and compare again
Termination remains Active or credential remains Available
Retry only with the current generation; inspect controller, broker, helper, and notification evidence
Never return the node to managed service
Quarantine, alert, preserve evidence, and run the approved recovery procedure
Open the protected readiness details and close every named external or internal gate

blocks.question: What is the final acceptance condition?
blocks.answer: Every visited page renders without an owned UI error; each consequential action reaches its documented next state; MoonLeaf preserves the selected template, Chinese text, spacing, and field ownership; the installer reconciles exactly the explicitly selected deployment scope; and production release remains blocked until protected readiness and external evidence are green.

pages.title: 50-scenario production UI validation
pages.summary: The evidence ledger for 50 atomic UI journeys across the installer, operator console, enterprise portal, MoonLeaf contracts, machine access, notifications, catalog, and workbench — with a hard line between what was really demonstrated, what is demo-only, and what is still blocked.
pages.audience: Release owner, acceptance tester, platform operator, and risk reviewer

blocks.text: What we actually proved

blocks.title: 42 scoped passes; 8 production observations still blocked
blocks.text: Ten journeys exercised a real local boundary, and 32 exercised clearly labelled demo behavior. Seven are still waiting on real infrastructure, and one responsive-layout check is blocked by the browser harness itself. Nothing was promoted: no demo action, disabled button, Colima preview, or synthetic credential was counted as a real-cluster result.

rows: The browser drove a real local boundary — the native installer companion, the saved language preference, input validation, or a client that fails closed.
The browser drove the real interface — rendering, state changes, confirmations, role separation, guards — against a snapshot that is clearly labelled as non-authoritative.
The journey is defined, but the physical hardware or an external system was not there. This is not a pass.
The controlled browser did not apply the requested responsive viewport reliably. We did not substitute automated CSS checks for the missing observation.

blocks.text: What the 50 scenarios cover

rows: All 17 routes; 4/4 machines and nine-model demo provenance; destructive confirmations; users, leases, catalog, deployments, requests, audit, model evidence, plus injection and length boundaries.
All nine routes; tenant boundary; contract ownership; renewal; obligations; notifications; credential redemption; exact-phrase early termination; cleanup presentation.

Incomplete-input gate; local-mode reduction; a real native dry-run preview; wrong-token terminal reset; the exact confirmation phrase. Apply was deliberately never clicked — it would change the local system.
All seven source forms and 18 physical pages; Chinese rendering; operator/customer field separation; automatic preview refresh; approval evidence and rejection reasons.
Missing-token gate; insecure-origin rejection; a bounded failure with no token leakage. The production invoke, stream, cancel, rate-limit, and expiry paths stay on the external-blocker list.
Script text, identifier boundaries, stale output, exact destructive phrases, hidden credentials, demo non-mutation, renewal predecessor retention, and blocked physical-reclaim proof.

blocks.text: Bugs the campaign found — and we fixed

items: A rejected installer run no longer leaves an old success transcript on screen.
Demo credential redemption now ends with an explicit synthetic, secret-free handoff instead of spinning forever.
The customer lease form now rejects reserved Unix usernames with the same rule the backend uses.
Notification timestamps now show a readable UTC date instead of raw epoch milliseconds.

blocks.text: Production blockers that are still real

items: A physical four-DGX exercise: enrollment, NVIDIA/ARM64 runtime, saturation, drain, thermal, long streams, and failures.
Production identity and mTLS with two real operators; a credential issuer or SSH CA; the root helper; exact-generation revocation; sanitization, quarantine, and physical reclaim evidence.

HA PostgreSQL with encrypted backup and restore and measured RPO/RTO; external notification delivery; telemetry export; object storage, scanner, and renderer/font baseline; legal and finance approvals; entitlement authority.
A production workbench workload that proves admission ownership, streaming, cancellation, rate-limit recovery, and lease expiry against real serving adapters.
A real 390 px and 200%-zoom browser run kept with screenshots; the controlled-viewport observation was inconclusive.

blocks.text: The wider gap to a full GPU cloud

The honest near-term goal is a well-run private GPU cloud, not immediate AWS feature parity. Close physical acceptance, HA authority, identity, networking, storage, metering, billing, incident ownership, and support operations first. Regions, spot capacity, training, and a marketplace come later.

rows: Repeatable physical-cluster acceptance; production trust and destructive reclaim; HA data restore; real external adapters; named 24×7 operations and release authority.

Tenant-visible quotas and reservations; pricing and immutable usage records; invoices, refunds, and disputes; network, storage, and image lifecycle; stable API/CLI/SDK; search, tags, support cases, and audit export.
Multi-site failure domains, autoscaling, spot and preemptible supply, training, marketplace, organization federation, and advanced FinOps — only after P0 and P1 are repeatable.

blocks.title: The full ledger
blocks.text: The repository page docs/UI_PRODUCTION_VALIDATION_50_SCENARIOS.md is the authoritative record: every click sequence, expected and observed result, evidence class, all eight blockers, the four fixes, and the AWS-like capability comparison.

blocks.question: When may a blocked scenario become a pass?
blocks.answer: Only after the same UI journey is repeated against the real dependency — and the operator identity, timestamps, audit receipts, runtime and artifact digests, cluster revision, screenshots, and external evidence are all kept together.

pages.title: Watch the system, back it up, and recover it
pages.summary: How to keep an eye on LunaNexa day to day, what to back up so a disaster is survivable, and how to bring a controller back safely: read-only first, normal operation only after state and reality agree.
pages.audience: On-call operators and whoever owns disaster recovery

blocks.text: Use this page in two moments: the quiet ones, when you want to know the platform is healthy, and the bad ones, when the controller or its data is gone and you have to bring it back. The rule for the bad moments is simple: look first, change later.
Watch first, change later

items: The controller's /health and /version, checked through the trusted management network — never from the public internet.
The /metrics endpoint, which only the dedicated monitoring credential may read.
Whether nodes keep their heartbeats fresh, and which deployments they report as ready.
GPU health, queue depth, and the small telemetry set the nodes send home.
What deployment operations found, which assignment generation is current, and whether runtimes are healthy.
Audit receipts for every important change — written once, never rewritten.
Workspace admission state: who holds concurrency, the rolling-hour counters, and when leases expire.

blocks.text: Back up everything that makes decisions

One backup has to cover everything the controller knows: PostgreSQL, plus the registry, scheduler, assignment, enrollment, telemetry, deployment, workspace admission, and exclusive-lease state files. Back up /data/models and the model signatures separately, on their own schedule. Encrypt every backup, and rehearse a restore now and then — a backup file that merely exists proves nothing until you have restored it.
Recovery is slow on purpose

steps.title: Fence the old writer
steps.text: Stop or isolate the old controller so nothing else can write. Restore the data onto clean infrastructure.

steps.title: Start with a newer epoch
steps.text: Bring the new controller up with a strictly higher LUNANEXA_CONTROLLER_EPOCH. Any old process loses its right to write.

steps.title: Look, don't touch
steps.text: Set LUNANEXA_RECONCILIATION_ONLY=1 and read /v1/recovery/plan before allowing any write.

steps.title: Compare with reality
steps.text: Work through missing assignments, expired leases, orphaned runtimes, receipts for work still running, and nodes that do not answer.

steps.title: Return to normal
steps.text: Resume normal operation only after the audit trail is continuous and repeated actions are provably safe.

blocks.title: Do not replay live work on faith
blocks.text: If a customer request was running when things broke, two things decide what to do: the durable workload receipt, and the serving adapter's own duplicate protection. Check both before you clear a quota or rebuild an execution.

blocks.question: The controller is gone. What is the first thing its replacement does?
blocks.answer: Nothing that writes. You start it with a newer epoch in reconciliation-only mode, compare the recovery plan with what is really out there, and allow writes only after stored state and observed reality agree.

pages.title: Debug controller, ingress, and fencing failures
pages.summary: Start from what you can actually see — a console that will not load, a rejected write, an Unauthenticated reply — and narrow down from there. Most controller trouble is process health, trusted ingress, configuration, networking, or epoch fencing.
pages.audience: On-call operator

blocks.text: Reach for this page when the console will not load, API calls bounce, or a controller misbehaves after a restart or restore. Each section starts from the symptom you can see and then narrows down. One rule holds throughout: never fix a problem by widening who can reach the controller.

blocks.symptom: The console will not load and the controller's health endpoint does not answer.
likely_causes: The controller pod is not ready, or it keeps crashing.
Something it needs at startup is missing: a rendered setting, a secret reference, a volume, or the PostgreSQL address.
The ingress route or network policy does not reach the controller.
The browser is going around the trusted ingress instead of through it.
checks: Look at the pod's status and readiness events, then the controller logs — they stay small on purpose.
Check that every placeholder in the deployment rendered to a real value, and that the controller is scheduled on a management node.
Probe /health from an allowed management pod first, then through the trusted ingress.
Confirm PostgreSQL is up and the controller can connect — without printing the database URL anywhere.
resolution: Fix the one thing that is actually broken — rendering, storage, database, or routing — and let Kubernetes restart the pod normally.
Keep direct public access to the controller blocked. Repair the ingress or policy; do not open the controller up instead.
escalate_when: The controller keeps corrupting or rejecting its own saved state.
Getting healthy again takes a restore or an epoch change — move to the recovery page.

blocks.symptom: A change you submit comes back as StaleControllerEpoch.
likely_causes: A newer controller has already taken over and moved the fencing epoch forward.
An old controller process, an old assignment, or a restored snapshot is trying to write.
checks: Check the current epoch in the durable store and which controller is active.
Make sure no old controller process or pod is still reachable.
Open /v1/recovery/plan from the newer controller, running in reconciliation-only mode.
resolution: Never lower the epoch or reuse an old one. Cut the stale writer off and continue from the newer epoch.
escalate_when: Two live controllers both seem to be in charge.
The durable store and the running deployment disagree about the current epoch.

blocks.symptom: Calls from a browser or remote client come back Unauthenticated.
likely_causes: The credential being sent is missing, or it is the wrong kind for this route — operator, inference, audit, or monitoring.
Ingress did not check the client certificate, or it did not inject the verified identity headers.
A remote client tried to send X-LunaNexa-Subject directly. That header is only accepted from loopback.
checks: Check which credential this route expects, without echoing the secret itself.
Look at what the ingress did with authentication and whether it overwrites identity headers.
Confirm the controller sees the request arriving from the trusted network path.
resolution: Issue or route the right scoped credential through the trusted identity boundary. Never loosen the subject-header rule for remote callers.
escalate_when: Any caller manages to fake an identity or reach a scope it should not have.

blocks.symptom: The administrator diagnostics page in the guide is missing, stale, or shows gaps.
likely_causes: The trusted identity proxy did not re-sign the operator headers, or signed them too long ago.
The skill manifest or the coursebook evidence index is invalid, or older than its freshness limit.
One of the internal read-only endpoints behind diagnostics is down.
A required secret reference — the HMAC key or the controller credential — is absent.
checks: Open /health and look only at the admin_diagnostics flag.
Use the reference number from admin.html to find the matching GuideAdminDiagnosticRequest audit event.
Confirm the identity proxy signs exactly the documented fields, without printing its HMAC key.
Confirm the internal route exposes only the five fixed read endpoints, and that every skill lists its version, required evidence, allowed data, and runbook.
resolution: Repair whichever piece is marked missing — proxy, secret reference, HTTPS route, coursebook index, or controller endpoint — then refresh admin.html.
If you cannot run a trusted proxy and the internal HTTPS gateway, leave administrator diagnostics off. The public coursebook and the read-only guide keep working without it.
escalate_when: The public guide can see live cluster state, an administrator answer names a node, user, or lease, or any response leaks prompts, logs, credentials, or reasoning traces.

pages.title: Debug missing nodes, blocked placement, and runtimes
pages.summary: A node in the inventory only proves it enrolled — not that a model can run there. Work through identity, scheduler eligibility, artifact checks, runtime health, and routing, one layer at a time, starting from the symptom you see.
pages.audience: DGX and model-runtime operator

blocks.text: Use this page when a machine goes missing from the fleet, a deployment cannot find a home, or a model runtime refuses to become ready. Watch out for the classic trap: a node appearing in the inventory only proves it enrolled. It says nothing about whether a model can actually run there.

blocks.symptom: A DGX is missing from the fleet, or it has flipped to Unreachable.
likely_causes: The three names for the same machine disagree: the Kubernetes node name, LUNANEXA_NODE_ID, and the inventory node_id.
The bootstrap material expired or was replayed, or the node's long-term credential is wrong.
The heartbeat was rejected — transport, certificate, clock, generation, or replay protection.
The node agent is stopped, or it cannot read its protected files on the host.
checks: Check the Kubernetes node name and its GPU label.
Look at the node-agent service or pod and its logs.
Check certificate expiry and clock skew, the last accepted heartbeat, and the rejection code in the controller's audit log.
Confirm the credential files exist, are unique to this node, and have the right ownership — without printing their contents.
resolution: Fix the identity or host material, rotate through the documented certificate or bootstrap path, and wait for a fresh, authenticated heartbeat.
escalate_when: You suspect a credential was copied, or a heartbeat was forged or replayed.
A leased node's watchdog or helper process is running unprotected.

blocks.symptom: A deployment sits at Blocked, or no node is eligible.
likely_causes: Review evidence is missing: license, evaluation, approval, signature, secret reference, or data class.
A hard filter fails — GPU architecture, memory, runtime, model, lease, or node state.
The node is cordoned, draining, unreachable, or exclusively leased, or its heartbeat has not reported the exact ready deployment.
checks: Read the preflight findings and the scheduler's placement reasoning — they say exactly which rule failed.
Compare the artifact and runtime digests you asked for with the approved alias and the node's live heartbeat.
Check free GPU memory, GPU health, labels, taints, lease mode, and whether the node has a route.
resolution: Supply the missing reviewed evidence, or restore real capacity and readiness. Never edit labels to make a node pretend a runtime is ready.
escalate_when: The same inputs produce different placement decisions, or a hard filter was bypassed.

blocks.symptom: Calls end with RuntimeUnavailable, or readiness never settles.
likely_causes: The model artifact failed a size, digest, or signature check.
The digest-pinned image is missing, built for the wrong architecture, swapped out, lacks a health check, or keeps exiting.
The node's strict endpoint is absent, or TLS and network policy block it.
The serving API does not match the adapter contract LunaNexa is configured for.
checks: Read the materialization and quarantine receipts.
Verify the exact image identity and its built-in health check, without exposing credentials.
Probe the runtime from the approved path and compare its /health and compatibility endpoint.
Confirm the node appears in the strict HTTPS route document.
resolution: Fix or requalify the artifact, image, or route, then publish a new reviewed template or assignment generation. Do not fall back to mutable tags or generic routing.
escalate_when: The image digest differs between registry, assignment, node cache, and what is actually running.
The runtime's public error message leaks internal paths or credentials.

pages.title: Debug workspace access and PostgreSQL
pages.summary: When someone is told no by a workspace, when limits trip, or when the controller cannot talk to PostgreSQL. Most denials are the platform working as designed — the job is to find which rule said no, not to switch the rule off.
pages.audience: Access administrator and database operator

blocks.text: Use this page when a workspace refuses someone, when rate or concurrency limits trip, or when the controller cannot reach its database. Fair warning first: most access denials are the platform working exactly as designed. Your job is to find out which rule said no — not to switch the rule off.

likely_causes: The caller's identity is not recognized, or the ingress identity mapping changed.
The user is invited, suspended, or revoked — not active.
The grant is missing, revoked, expired, or belongs to another tenant.
The lease is the wrong kind, outside its time window, expired, revoked, or still only requested.
Permissions changed between the moment the user read their state and the moment they called.
checks: Read /v1/workspace/self through the same trusted identity path the caller used.
In the console, look at the exact user, grant, tenant, lease state, capability, and the start and expiry times.
Read the audit events before and after any recent activation, suspension, revocation, or end.
resolution: Fix the authoritative record through the operator lifecycle route. Never forge an identity header, and never edit the state file by hand.
escalate_when: A revoked caller can still invoke, or one tenant can see another tenant's work.

blocks.symptom: Calls come back WorkspaceConcurrencyExceeded or WorkspaceRateExceeded.
likely_causes: All of the capability's concurrent slots are currently held.
The rolling one-hour request limit is used up.
A controller crash left a reservation held until its deadline — that is deliberate, not a bug.
checks: Look at which workloads are active and who may cancel them.
Review the admissions state or the PostgreSQL snapshot with operator tooling. Do not delete anything.
Confirm the deadlines and the release of finished or cancelled work are being reconciled.
resolution: Wait for the held slot to expire, cancel a workload you own, or approve a lease change. Never clear counters by deleting durable records.
escalate_when: A finished workload never releases its slot, even after recovery.

blocks.symptom: The controller cannot start, or cannot write to its PostgreSQL-backed state.
likely_causes: The database URL, TLS verification, network policy, role privileges, or schema version is wrong.
The migration was run without owner authority — or not run at all.
A constraint on a normalized table rejected the transaction.
checks: Probe PostgreSQL readiness from the controller's own network.
Run the idempotent migration command with the secret reference and the owner role.
After a restore, check schema_migrations and the projection row counts.
Read the (deliberately short) database error without printing the URL or password.
resolution: Fix the secret-provider value, TLS trust, network rule, role, or migration — then rerun the transaction once the schema is valid.
escalate_when: The snapshot and the normalized tables disagree, or a failed write left partial state behind.

pages.title: Configuration map
pages.summary: Every LunaNexa setting lives in the deployment, not in the product. This page maps the knobs by area and states the safety rule for each: credentials come from a secret provider, and public manifests carry references and digests, never values.
pages.audience: Deployment engineer

blocks.text: Use this page when you are standing up a deployment and need to know which settings exist and which rules keep them safe. Two principles cover almost everything: configuration belongs to the deployment, and secrets never appear in the repository — manifests name a reference, the secret provider holds the value.

rows: LUNANEXA_STATE_PATH, REGISTRY_PATH, ENROLLMENT_PATH, SCHEDULER_PATH, TELEMETRY_PATH, DEPLOYMENT_PATH
Back them up as one set. Use absolute, protected paths, and fence writers with epochs.
Use postgres in production. The URL comes from the secret provider, with TLS verification.
One scope per token. Tokens never appear in the repository, URLs, logs, or browser storage.
deploy/oidc-browser-ingress.yaml; secret lunanexa-identity-ingress-credentials; controller key account-session-issuer-secret; LUNANEXA_ACCOUNT_PATH=/var/lib/lunanexa/accounts.json
These are reference names only. The values behind them stay in the secret provider.
Each is an independent authority. A node receives only the matching verifier.
Every schedulable node gets one strict HTTPS route. There is no generic fallback.
A node pulls only what was assigned to it. The runtime never sees the artifact credential.
Raise the epoch monotonically, and read the recovery plan before allowing writes.

blocks.title: Administrator settings win
blocks.text: Once the validated administrator settings document is configured, the legacy environment overrides for admission and runtime concurrency are migration fallbacks — not a second source of truth competing with it.

blocks.title: Never publish values from a real cluster
blocks.text: This coursebook names settings and what they mean — nothing more. It must never contain real hosts, private addresses, database URLs, node inventories, tokens, keys, certificates, or resolved secret references.

pages.title: Public error and state reference
pages.summary: What each public error code and state means, whether retrying helps, and what to do next. The messages are short on purpose — they tell you which boundary said no, never what the cluster looks like inside.
pages.audience: Client developer and on-call operator

blocks.text: Use this page when an API call or the UI answers with a code you do not recognize. The code tells you which boundary rejected the work and whether a retry makes sense; the table then points you at the right diagnostic path. Do not read topology into a deliberately short public message.

rows: Required scoped credential or verified subject is absent/invalid
Fix the trusted identity or credential path; do not retry blindly.
Authenticated authority lacks the requested scope
Use the right scoped credential or request an explicit grant.
Subject, user, grant, tenant, lease, capability, or ownership does not authorize the request
Capability's held concurrent requests are in use
Wait, cancel an owned workload, or review lease capacity.
Rolling one-hour request limit is exhausted
Wait for the window or apply a reviewed lease change.
Same active workload/idempotency scope already exists
Query the existing workload; do not launch a duplicate.
Treat as terminal for that request; reassess deadline/capacity before a new logical operation.
Selected serving adapter failed or disappeared
Inspect artifact, image, readiness, route, TLS, and adapter compatibility.
A newer durable controller fenced this writer or assignment
Fence the stale process and reconcile under the newer epoch.
Node is absent or already bound by incompatible authority
Inspect enrollment, heartbeat, lease, and current node mode.
Preflight evidence or capacity is missing
Read typed findings; supply reviewed evidence before retrying.
The authenticated owner cancelled the workload
No runtime-failure escalation unless cancellation was unexpected.

blocks.title: Public errors stay short on purpose
blocks.text: They never contain node addresses, filesystem paths, container IDs, provider credentials, stack traces, or internal topology. When you need more, operators correlate the audit trail and read the protected logs.

pages.title: P0/P1/P2 expansion and offering launch plan
pages.summary: A deployable four-node repository is not the same as a product you can sell. This page separates the internal pilot, the managed-inference launch, the dedicated-workspace launch, and later private-cloud breadth — each with the external evidence it still needs and a code-size planning range.
pages.audience: Product owner, engineering lead, deployment owner, security reviewer, and release board

blocks.text: The current four-node verdict

blocks.text: Expect 30–40% of the expansion to be tests, fault injection, recovery, and retained acceptance evidence. Most production growth belongs in the durable controllers — capacity, quota, network, storage, image — plus identity and policy, metering and billing, external adapters, and operations. The UI and clients should stay a thin projection layer.
Recommended phase order

blocks.title: From repository baseline to private GPU cloud

steps.title: Phase 0 · Preserve baseline
steps.text: Keep the typed boundaries, release tests, simulation, leak scans, and the honest 50-scenario UI ledger green.

steps.title: Phase 1 · Four-node internal pilot
steps.text: Deploy the physical fleet, qualify real runtimes, exercise failures and restore, and obtain named internal acceptance.

steps.title: Phase 2 · Shared production foundations
steps.text: Browser sign-in with OIDC and human accounts is already built. What remains is your deployment's gateway image and production IdP, authority separation, HA data, live delivery and export, quotas, SLOs, and incident ownership.

steps.title: Phase 3 · Managed inference launch
steps.text: Prove real customer invocation, streaming, cancellation, metering, pricing, capacity, and support under production identity.

steps.title: Phase 4 · Dedicated workspace launch
steps.text: Prove credential issuance, offline expiry, revocation, destructive sanitization, quarantine, and machine reclaim on the exact host image.

steps.title: Phase 5 · Focused P1
steps.text: Add only the required IAM, reservations, network and storage profiles, image lifecycle, billing, SDK, and support resources.

steps.title: Phase 6 · Selective P2
steps.text: Treat multi-site, autoscaling, spot, training, marketplace, and advanced FinOps as independent programs after demand and operations are proven.

blocks.text: Integrate infrastructure; build GPU authority

items: Use Kubernetes for workload orchestration, and established providers for identity, secrets, networking, storage, PostgreSQL, telemetry, payment, invoicing, and signature.
LunaNexa owns the GPU-specific part: desired state, model and runtime governance, capacity admission, lease policy, exclusive-access fencing, evidence, and reconciliation.
Do not turn LunaNexa into an identity provider, an object store, a virtual network, a payment gateway, a container engine, or a metrics database.

blocks.title: Commercial wording follows evidence
blocks.text: Until the managed-inference Phase 3 is accepted, call LunaNexa an internal platform or a deployment candidate. Until the dedicated-workspace Phase 4 is accepted, do not issue customer machine credentials. A contract, invoice, or UI status cannot override these operational gates.

blocks.question: What is the next real milestone?
blocks.answer: Complete the physical four-node internal-pilot campaign. It converts repository and simulation evidence into environment-specific enrollment, runtime, performance, failure, restore, and named-human acceptance — without yet promising a customer SLA.

pages.title: How this coursebook was produced
pages.summary: This site is a reading projection of the LunaNexa repository, generated from its documents, contracts, and tests. The repository stays the source of truth; this page explains what the projection does, what it never does, and where to check exactly which revision it was built from.
pages.audience: Documentation reviewers and future maintainers

blocks.text: What this site is — and is not

The repository remains authoritative. This site re-organizes its evidence around reader questions and renders only structured text blocks. It does not execute authored HTML, it does not embed production state, and it never claims that generating documentation tested a real cluster.
How fresh is it?

blocks.title: Check the evidence ledger, not this prose
blocks.text: The exact source revision, dirty state, source digests, claim statuses, and known gaps are recorded in the evidence ledger (coursebook-evidence.json) shipped with this site. Treat that ledger as the source of truth for freshness. Whatever the revision, physical DGX enrollment, external adapter acceptance, production PostgreSQL, and named human approval remain separate deployment gates that no repository release implies.
The read-only Ask guide

The Ask guide panel is optional. A same-origin server sends the published coursebook and the public evidence projection to MoonClaw's existing read-only Cowork endpoint, and the adapter validates a narrow answer schema with known page citations. It cannot edit LunaNexa, run commands, expose gateway details, or stand in for operator authority.
Lessons adapted from the Suanli reference

items: Stable product-level navigation above a grouped documentation sidebar.
One focused article per page, with an on-page outline on the right.
Search kept prominent in the global header.
Clear routes for product overview, quickstart, usage, FAQ and debugging, best practices, and prebuilt runtimes.
LunaNexa adds its own layer on top: explicit evidence status, production gaps, trust boundaries, and this source ledger — rather than copying Suanli's brand or claims.

blocks.question: What should happen when LunaNexa source changes?
blocks.answer: Re-run the repository evidence scan, update source digests and claim statuses, regenerate coursebook.json, exercise the site and guide states, and review the meaning before publishing. The evidence ledger records which revision all of this was done against.
